claim: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are web-like chromatin structures composed by dsDNA and histones, decorated with antimicrobial proteins.
source: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are web-like chromatin structures composed by dsDNA and histones, decorated with antimicrobial proteins.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about NETs that draws from established scientific knowledge about their composition.

claim: The interaction of NETs with dendritic cells (DCs) allows DC activation and maturation toward presentation of NET-associated antigens.
source: Their interaction with dendritic cells (DCs) allows DC activation and maturation toward presentation of NET-associated antigens.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about NET-DC interactions and is referenced in the manuscript's prior work.

claim: NETosis preserves the proteins localized onto the DNA threads for proper enzymatic activity and conformational status, including immunogenic epitopes.
source: Differently from other types of cell death that imply protein denaturation, NETosis preserves the proteins localized onto the DNA threads for proper enzymatic activity and conformational status, including immunogenic epitopes.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the unique properties of NETosis based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Leukemic cells can release extracellular traps displaying leukemia-associated antigens.
source: Besides neutrophils, leukemic cells can release extracellular traps displaying leukemia-associated antigens, prototypically mutant nucleophosmin (NPMc+) that upon mutation translocates from nucleolus to the cytoplasm localizing onto NET threads.
evidence: This statement is supported by the authors' previous work and observations in this study.

claim: Mutant nucleophosmin (NPMc+) translocates from nucleolus to the cytoplasm upon mutation and localizes onto NET threads.
source: Besides neutrophils, leukemic cells can release extracellular traps displaying leukemia-associated antigens, prototypically mutant nucleophosmin (NPMc+) that upon mutation translocates from nucleolus to the cytoplasm localizing onto NET threads.
evidence: This describes the behavior of mutant NPM based on established knowledge and prior observations.

claim: Vaccination with DC loaded with NPMc+ NET (NPMc+ NET/DC) reduced myeloproliferation in transgenic mice.
source: Vaccination with DC loaded with NPMc+ NET (NPMc+ NET/DC) reduced myeloproliferation in transgenic mice, favoring the development of antibodies to mutant NPMc and the induction of a CD8+ T-cell response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination favored the development of antibodies to mutant NPMc.
source: Vaccination with DC loaded with NPMc+ NET (NPMc+ NET/DC) reduced myeloproliferation in transgenic mice, favoring the development of antibodies to mutant NPMc and the induction of a CD8+ T-cell response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data (ELISA results) presented in the manuscript.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination induced a CD8+ T-cell response.
source: Vaccination with DC loaded with NPMc+ NET (NPMc+ NET/DC) reduced myeloproliferation in transgenic mice, favoring the development of antibodies to mutant NPMc and the induction of a CD8+ T-cell response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data (flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry) presented in the manuscript.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination impaired the expansion of NPMc+ in favor of WT myeloid compartment in mixed NPMc/WT bone marrow chimeras.
source: The efficacy of this vaccine was also tested in mixed NPMc/WT bone marrow (BM) chimeras in a competitive BM transplantation setting, where the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination impaired the expansion of NPMc+ in favor of WT myeloid compartment.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from competitive bone marrow transplantation experiments.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination achieved control of an aggressive leukemia transduced with mutant NPMc.
source: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination also achieved control of an aggressive leukemia transduced with mutant NPMc, effectively inducing an antileukemia CD8 T-cell memory response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from C1498-NPMc+ leukemia model experiments.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination effectively induced an antileukemia CD8 T-cell memory response.
source: NPMc+ NET/DC vaccination also achieved control of an aggressive leukemia transduced with mutant NPMc, effectively inducing an antileukemia CD8 T-cell memory response.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing CD8 T-cell responses and memory markers.

claim: Volker Brinkmann showed spider web-like chromatin structures extruded by neutrophils for the first time fifteen years ago using scanning electron microscopy.
source: Fifteen years ago, a scanning electron microscopy image from Volker Brinkmann showed for the first time spider web-like chromatin structures extruded by neutrophils, called neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), to entrap fungi and bacteria (Brinkmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation to Brinkmann et al., 2004.

claim: NETs entrap fungi and bacteria.
source: Fifteen years ago, a scanning electron microscopy image from Volker Brinkmann showed for the first time spider web-like chromatin structures extruded by neutrophils, called neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), to entrap fungi and bacteria (Brinkmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a functional statement about NETs supported by citation to Brinkmann et al., 2004.

claim: Extracellular chromatin is decorated with antimicrobial proteins like myeloperoxidase (MPO) and neutrophil elastase.
source: Such extracellular chromatin is composed by DNA and histones also decorated with antimicrobial proteins like myeloperoxidase (MPO) and neutrophil elastase suggesting the hypothesis that eukaryotic chromatin evolved under the need of maintaining genome integrity while defending the organism (Brinkmann and Zychlinsky, 2012).
evidence: This is a compositional statement about NETs supported by citation to Brinkmann and Zychlinsky, 2012.

claim: Eukaryotic chromatin evolved under the need of maintaining genome integrity while defending the organism.
source: Such extracellular chromatin is composed by DNA and histones also decorated with antimicrobial proteins like myeloperoxidase (MPO) and neutrophil elastase suggesting the hypothesis that eukaryotic chromatin evolved under the need of maintaining genome integrity while defending the organism (Brinkmann and Zychlinsky, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about chromatin evolution supported by citation.

claim: Extracellular traps can be released by eosinophils, macrophages, and mast cells.
source: Extracellular traps can be released by other innate immune cells including eosinophils, macrophages, and mast cells (Goldmann and Medina, 2012) and, as recently shown, by cells of the adaptive immunity like CD4 T-helper cells (Costanza et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Goldmann and Medina, 2012.

claim: CD4 T-helper cells can release extracellular traps.
source: Extracellular traps can be released by other innate immune cells including eosinophils, macrophages, and mast cells (Goldmann and Medina, 2012) and, as recently shown, by cells of the adaptive immunity like CD4 T-helper cells (Costanza et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Costanza et al., 2019.

claim: NET has been associated with inflammatory and immune-mediated diseases like diabetes, arthritis, systemic vasculitis, and lupus erythematosus.
source: Additionally, since their discovery, NET has been associated with inflammatory and immune-mediated diseases like diabetes, arthritis, systemic vasculitis, and lupus erythematosus (Jorch and Kubes, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jorch and Kubes, 2017.

claim: NET-based dendritic cell (DC) vaccination was able to break tolerance against neutrophil cytoplasmatic antigens and induce antineutrophil cytoplasmatic antibodies (ANCA)-associated autoimmunity.
source: In a previous study, we demonstrated that the adoption of a NET-based dendritic cell (DC) vaccination was able to break tolerance against neutrophil cytoplasmatic antigens and induce antineutrophil cytoplasmatic antibodies (ANCA)-associated autoimmunity.
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: NET is highly immunogenic by virtue of the immune adjuvant effect of DNA and its associated proteins.
source: Indeed, NET is highly immunogenic by virtue of the immune adjuvant effect of DNA and its associated proteins, as well as for the sticky properties of the DNA thread that enable NET persistent interaction with DCs for efficient loading of antigens followed by DC maturation and migration to draining lymph nodes for cross-presentation (Sangaletti et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sangaletti et al., 2012.

claim: The sticky properties of the DNA thread enable NET persistent interaction with DCs for efficient loading of antigens followed by DC maturation and migration to draining lymph nodes for cross-presentation.
source: Indeed, NET is highly immunogenic by virtue of the immune adjuvant effect of DNA and its associated proteins, as well as for the sticky properties of the DNA thread that enable NET persistent interaction with DCs for efficient loading of antigens followed by DC maturation and migration to draining lymph nodes for cross-presentation (Sangaletti et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sangaletti et al., 2012.

claim: Myeloid transformed cells can extrude NET into the extracellular space to activate the contact system of coagulation.
source: Also, myeloid transformed cells can extrude NET into the extracellular space to activate the contact system of coagulation (Demers et al., 2012) or to sustain myeloproliferation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Demers et al., 2012.

claim: Myeloid transformed cells can extrude NET into the extracellular space to sustain myeloproliferation.
source: Also, myeloid transformed cells can extrude NET into the extracellular space to activate the contact system of coagulation (Demers et al., 2012) or to sustain myeloproliferation.
evidence: This statement is based on the authors' work and observations.

claim: Extracellular traps enrichment has been described in bone marrow (BM) biopsies from NPM1 mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients.
source: We have recently described extracellular traps enrichment in bone marrow (BM) biopsies from NPM1 mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients and, using an ad hoc transgenic mouse, we showed that NPM cytoplasmic compartmentalization allows mutant NPM (NPMc+) to be relocalized onto the NET threads, exerting alarmin functions (Tripodo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous work supported by citation to Tripodo et al., 2017.

claim: NPM cytoplasmic compartmentalization allows mutant NPM (NPMc+) to be relocalized onto the NET threads, exerting alarmin functions.
source: We have recently described extracellular traps enrichment in bone marrow (BM) biopsies from NPM1 mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients and, using an ad hoc transgenic mouse, we showed that NPM cytoplasmic compartmentalization allows mutant NPM (NPMc+) to be relocalized onto the NET threads, exerting alarmin functions (Tripodo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous work supported by citation to Tripodo et al., 2017.

claim: The colocalization of histones with NPMc+ is a supporting evidence of their direct release from the leukemic clone.
source: The colocalization of histones with NPMc+ is a supporting evidence of their direct release from the leukemic clone.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on observations and logical inference.

claim: The immune system has the capacity to eradicate AML as shown by the graft-versus-leukemia effect that is obtained after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
source: The immune system has the capacity to eradicate AML as shown by the graft-versus-leukemia effect that is obtained after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
evidence: This statement is based on established clinical knowledge about graft-versus-leukemia effects.

claim: Ideal immune molecular targets of AML should be restricted to leukemic cells including stem cells and be part of leukemic development.
source: Accordingly, ideal immune molecular targets of AML should be restricted to leukemic cells including stem cells and be part of leukemic development.
evidence: This is a logical inference about ideal therapeutic targets based on established principles.

claim: Leukemia-associated antigens such as RHAMM, Proteinase 3, and Wilms' tumor antigen-1 (WT-1) have entered clinical trials as peptide vaccines.
source: Indeed, the leukemia-associated antigens that entered clinical trials as peptide vaccines, such as RHAMM, Proteinase 3, and Wilms' tumor antigen-1 (WT-1), possess these features (Anguille et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Anguille et al., 2012.

claim: NPM1 mutations are among the most frequent molecular alterations in AML.
source: NPM1 mutations are among the most frequent molecular alterations in AML, where they play a prognostic role (Falini et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Falini et al., 2005.

claim: NPM1 mutations play a prognostic role in AML.
source: NPM1 mutations are among the most frequent molecular alterations in AML, where they play a prognostic role (Falini et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Falini et al., 2005.

claim: NPM1 gene encodes for the nucleolar protein nucleophosmin that regulates the ARF-p53 tumor-suppressor pathway.
source: NPM1 gene encodes for the nucleolar protein nucleophosmin that regulates the ARF-p53 tumor-suppressor pathway (Colombo et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Colombo et al., 2011.

claim: NPMc mutations cause the stable relocalization of the protein from nucleus to cytoplasm.
source: NPMc mutations cause the stable relocalization of the protein from nucleus to cytoplasm, an event that, per se, is sufficient to trigger AML (Falini et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Falini et al., 2007.

claim: NPMc relocalization from nucleus to cytoplasm is sufficient to trigger AML.
source: NPMc mutations cause the stable relocalization of the protein from nucleus to cytoplasm, an event that, per se, is sufficient to trigger AML (Falini et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Falini et al., 2007.

claim: The improved overall survival of patients with NPMc+ AML has been possibly explained by a T-cell response against the mutant epitopes.
source: The improved overall survival of patients with NPMc+ AML has been possibly explained by a T-cell response against the mutant epitopes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of improved survival.

claim: The specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell response against NPMc epitopes raised the possibility of exploiting such property to immunize NPMc+ patients to control MRD or during maintenance treatment.
source: The specific CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell response against these epitopes raised the possibility of exploiting such property to immunize NPMc+ patients to control MRD or during maintenance treatment (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Schneider et al., 2014.

claim: NET directly released by leukemic cells could efficiently display tumor-specific associated antigens and be used as vehicles for new DC-based vaccines.
source: In this context, NET directly released by leukemic cells could efficiently display tumor-specific associated antigens and be used as vehicles for new DC-based vaccines.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential application of NETs in vaccination.

claim: The h-MRP8-NPM1+ (NPMc+) transgenic mice develop a myeloproliferation with expansion of mature CD11b+ myeloid cells and Gr-1+c-Kit+ myeloblasts, without development of overt acute leukemia.
source: The h-MRP8-NPM1+ (NPMc+) transgenic mice develop a myeloproliferation with expansion of mature CD11b+ myeloid cells and Gr-1+c-Kit+ myeloblasts, without development of overt acute leukemia.
evidence: This is a characterization of the transgenic mouse model based on observations.

claim: Mutant NPM can work as an alarmin when localized in the cytoplasm as part of the NET thread.
source: Using NET from NPMc+ transgenic mice we previously demonstrated that mutant NPM can work as an alarmin when localized in the cytoplasm as part of the NET thread (Swerdlow et al., 2016), gaining immunogenicity.
evidence: This statement refers to the authors' previous work supported by citation to Swerdlow et al., 2016.

claim: During coculture, DC became loaded with the prototypical NET-associated antigen MPO.
source: During coculture, DC became loaded with the prototypical NET-associated antigen MPO (Figure 1B, red signal) and, only in case of NPMc+ NET, with mutant NPMc (Figure 1B, green signal).
evidence: This is an observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DC became loaded with mutant NPMc only in case of NPMc+ NET coculture.
source: During coculture, DC became loaded with the prototypical NET-associated antigen MPO (Figure 1B, red signal) and, only in case of NPMc+ NET, with mutant NPMc (Figure 1B, green signal).
evidence: This is an observation supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC immunization conspicuously reduced the signs of myeloid expansion in the BM of NPMc+ mice, with a decrease in dense clusters of morphologically immature granulocytic elements.
source: NPMc+ NET/DC immunization, but not immunization with WT NET/DC, conspicuously reduced the signs of myeloid expansion in the BM of NPMc+ mice, with a decrease in dense clusters of morphologically immature granulocytic elements, as shown by histopathological analysis of H&E-stained BM sections (Figure 1C), and a reduction of myeloid blasts, in favor of more segmented forms on BM blood smears (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC immunization resulted in a reduction of myeloid blasts, in favor of more segmented forms on BM blood smears.
source: NPMc+ NET/DC immunization, but not immunization with WT NET/DC, conspicuously reduced the signs of myeloid expansion in the BM of NPMc+ mice, with a decrease in dense clusters of morphologically immature granulocytic elements, as shown by histopathological analysis of H&E-stained BM sections (Figure 1C), and a reduction of myeloid blasts, in favor of more segmented forms on BM blood smears (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by blood smear data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: NPMc+ NET immunization resulted in a significant decrease of cytoplasmic NPM-expressing elements.
source: Moreover, NPMc+ NET immunization resulted in a significant decrease of cytoplasmic NPM-expressing elements, as assessed by immunofluorescence (Figure 1E, F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: FACS analysis of the PB confirmed the reduction of circulating immature GR-1+c-Kit+ precursors in vaccinated mice.
source: Accordingly, Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) analysis of the PB confirmed the reduction of circulating immature GR-1+c-Kit+ precursors and of the overall frequency of CD11b+ cells (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—source data 2) in the same vaccinated mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1G, H.

claim: FACS analysis of the PB confirmed the reduction of the overall frequency of CD11b+ cells in vaccinated mice.
source: Accordingly, Fluorescence Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) analysis of the PB confirmed the reduction of circulating immature GR-1+c-Kit+ precursors and of the overall frequency of CD11b+ cells (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—source data 2) in the same vaccinated mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1G, H.

claim: The immune response triggered by NPMc+ NET immunization induced anti-NPMc+ serum antibodies detected by ELISA.
source: The immune response triggered by NPMc+ NET immunization induced anti-NPMc+ serum antibodies detected by ELISA (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 3) and the increase of CD8+ T-cells frequency in BM infiltrates (not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The immune response triggered by NPMc+ NET immunization increased CD8+ T-cells frequency in BM infiltrates.
source: The immune response triggered by NPMc+ NET immunization induced anti-NPMc+ serum antibodies detected by ELISA (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 3) and the increase of CD8+ T-cells frequency in BM infiltrates (not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding mentioned but not shown in figures.

claim: The increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells led to a higher frequency of CD8+ T cells closely contacting NPMc+ cells.
source: Of note, the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells led to a higher frequency of CD8+ T cells closely contacting NPMc+ cells (Figure 2A, B, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A, B.

claim: DC vaccination with NPMc+ NET is able to induce immune activation toward control of NPMc+ myeloproliferation.
source: Overall, these data indicate that DC vaccination with NPMc+ NET is able to induce immune activation toward control of NPMc+ myeloproliferation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Vaccination with NPMc+ NET-loaded DC impaired the expansion of CD45.1 mutant hematopoietic cells in favor of CD45.2 WT cells in the competitive setting.
source: Representative analysis (Figure 3B) and cumulative data (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1) show that vaccination with NPMc+ NET-loaded DC impaired the expansion of CD45.1 mutant hematopoietic cells in favor of CD45.2 WT cells in the competitive setting.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Vaccination with NET carrying mutant NPMc could selectively control the expansion of mutant cells derived from NPMc+ precursors, while sparing the normal counterpart.
source: These results suggest that vaccination with NET carrying mutant NPMc could selectively control the expansion of mutant cells derived from NPMc+ precursors, while sparing the normal counterpart.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the competitive BMT experimental data.

claim: The reduced expansion of CD45.1 NPMc+ cells was associated to increased CD8 T-cell infiltration in vaccinated mice.
source: Interestingly, the reduced expansion of CD45.1 NPMc+ cells was associated to increased CD8 T-cell infiltration in vaccinated mice (Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3D, E.

claim: The selective effect on mutant cells in the competitive setting underscores the efficacy and specificity of the engendered immune response toward mutant hematopoiesis.
source: The selective effect on mutant cells in the competitive setting underscores the efficacy and specificity of the engendered immune response toward mutant hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the competitive BMT experimental data.

claim: The immunization significantly delayed tumor growth in C1498-NPMc+ leukemia-bearing mice.
source: The immunization significantly delayed tumor growth (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1) and induced CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity against NPMc (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NPMc+ NET/DC immunization induced CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity against NPMc.
source: The immunization significantly delayed tumor growth (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1) and induced CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity against NPMc (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The NPMc +NET/DC vaccine induced a strong CD8+ T cytotoxic response in tumor-free mice.
source: In a different arm of the same experiment, the NPMc +NET/DC vaccine also induced a strong CD8+ T cytotoxic response in tumor-free mice (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine was superior to peptide-loaded DC in controlling tumor growth.
source: In a first set of experiments in which C1498-NPMc+ cells were injected subcutaneously, the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine was superior to peptide-loaded DC in controlling tumor growth (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In situ IHC analysis revealed increased tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and granzyme B+ elements in support of locally induced cytotoxic response, which was more robust in NPMc+ NET/DC than NPMc-derived MHC-I peptides/DC vaccinated mice.
source: In situ IHC analysis revealed increased tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and granzyme B+ elements in support of locally induced cytotoxic response, which was more robust in NPMc+ NET/DC than NPMc-derived MHC-I peptides/DC vaccinated mice (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—source data 4 and Figure 4—source data 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Results showed a reduction of GFP+ cells in the BM of mice vaccinated with either NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine or peptide/DC vaccine in comparison to nonvaccinated mice.
source: At end point, we evaluated the tumor take as the frequency of GFP+ leukemia cells in the BM. Results showed a reduction of GFP+ cells in the BM of mice vaccinated with either NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine or peptide/DC vaccine in comparison to nonvaccinated mice (Figure 4G and Figure 4—source data 6), which reached statistically significance in case of NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine (p = 0.0214 NPMc +NET/DC vs. ctrl and p = 0.0892 NPMc+ peptides vs. ctrl; Mann–Whitney t-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine was superior in inducing the proliferation of CD8 T cells compared to peptide/DC vaccine.
source: Despite similar frequency of CD8 T cell (Figure 4H, Figure 4—source data 7), the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine was superior in inducing the proliferation of CD8 T cells (Figure 4I, Figure 4—source data 8).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Both vaccines sustained OX40 expression on CD8 T cells.
source: Both vaccines sustained OX40 expression on CD8 T cells (Figure 4J, Figure 4—source data 9), however the reduction of exhausted PD1+TIM3+LAG3+ CD8 T cells (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 10) was higher in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The reduction of exhausted PD1+TIM3+LAG3+ CD8 T cells was higher in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
source: Both vaccines sustained OX40 expression on CD8 T cells (Figure 4J, Figure 4—source data 9), however the reduction of exhausted PD1+TIM3+LAG3+ CD8 T cells (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 10) was higher in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The production of TNF, but not IFNg, by CD8 T cells was higher in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
source: Accordingly, the production of TNF, but not IFNg, by CD8 T cells (Figure 4L–M, Figure 4—source data 11, and Figure 4—source data 12) was higher in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4L-M.

claim: A trend toward Tem increase was observed in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine.
source: Finally, a trend toward Tem increase was observed in mice receiving the NPMc+ NET/DC vaccine (Figure 4N, Figure 4—source data 13).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FACS data shown in Figure 4N.

claim: Both vaccines were able to induce Auto-Ab against mutant NPMc+.
source: ELISA assay showed that both vaccines were able to induce Auto-Ab against mutant NPMc+ (Figure 4O, Figure 4—source data 14), but only NPMc +NET/DC vaccinated mice developed Ab to MPO (Figure 4P, Figure 4—source data 15).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4O.

claim: Only NPMc +NET/DC vaccinated mice developed Ab to MPO.
source: ELISA assay showed that both vaccines were able to induce Auto-Ab against mutant NPMc+ (Figure 4O, Figure 4—source data 14), but only NPMc +NET/DC vaccinated mice developed Ab to MPO (Figure 4P, Figure 4—source data 15).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: These data support the efficacy of NET-based vaccines that were for some aspects superior in promoting T-cell responses in comparison to canonical peptide-based vaccines.
source: Overall these data support the efficacy of NET-based vaccines that were for some aspects superior in promoting T-cell responses in comparison to canonical peptide-based vaccines.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative experimental data presented.
